premise.title: Premise
premise.what: Your story in a sentence or two: who the protagonist is, what they want, what's stopping them and what they stand to lose. It's the compass to come back to when you get lost.

questions.q1: Who is your protagonist, in a few words?
questions.q2: What do they want, and why now?
questions.q3: Who or what gets in the way?
questions.q4: What do they lose if they fail?
questions.q5: What sets this story apart from the ones it resembles?

premise.example: Marta, a restorer, finds a portrait of her sister, missing for twenty years, beneath the fresco she's cleaning. To learn who painted it, she'll have to reopen a case her family wanted closed.

fabula.title: Fabula
fabula.what: The events of your story in chronological order, as they actually happened. The plot, by contrast, is the order you choose to tell them in: flashbacks, jumps ahead, delayed reveals.

questions.q1: Which event really sets everything off, even if it happens before the story starts?
questions.q2: In what order do things actually happen?
questions.q3: Which events do you tell out of order, and why?
questions.q4: Which facts stay offstage but still have to add up?

fabula.example: Fabula: Marta is born in 1962, her sister disappears in 1985, the fresco resurfaces in 2005. Plot: the novel opens in 2005 and reveals 1985 a piece at a time.

setting.title: Setting
setting.what: The where and when of your story: places, era, climate, social rules and, for invented worlds, the laws that govern them.

questions.q1: When and where does the story take place?
questions.q2: What makes this world different from the one we live in?
questions.q3: Which rules (social, political, magical, technological) can't be broken?
questions.q4: How does the setting change over the course of the story?
questions.q5: Which place could exist only in this story?

setting.example: Trieste, autumn 1913, after forty days of rain: the cafés are full of spies, the port is closed and the language changes from one street to the next.

strands.title: Narrative strands
strands.what: The lines of story that run through the work: the main plot, the subplots, the character arcs. Linking scenes to strands shows which ones are moving and which are falling behind.

questions.q1: What's the main plot, in one sentence?
questions.q2: Which subplots run alongside it, and what do they add to the theme?
questions.q3: Does every strand have a beginning, a middle and an end?
questions.q4: Where do the strands cross, and in which scenes?
questions.q5: Is there a strand you've dropped along the way?

strands.example: In a crime novel: the murder investigation (main plot), the inspector's failing marriage (subplot) and her trust in other people, which has to be rebuilt from scratch (arc).

quests.title: Quests
quests.what: In games, narrative strands become quests: the main quest carries the story to its end, side quests enrich it. Every quest has a giver, a list of objectives and a reward.

questions.q1: Who gives the quest, and why to the player?
questions.q2: What objectives make it up, and in what order?
questions.q3: What does the player gain beyond the reward?
questions.q4: What does this quest reveal about the world or a character?
questions.q5: What happens if the player ignores it, or fails?
questions.q6: Is it tied to other quests or to a variable?

quests.example: Side quest “The Dark Lighthouse”. Ilse, the keeper, asks you to relight the lamp. Objectives: find oil, mend the lens, hold out until dawn. Reward: a chart of the cliffs, and the story of her son.

pov.title: Point of view
pov.what: The eyes through which a scene is lived: who tells it, what they can know, how close we get to the characters' thoughts.

questions.q1: Who is best placed to tell this scene?
questions.q2: Who has the most to lose in it?
questions.q3: What needs to stay hidden, and which point of view allows it?
questions.q4: How close do you want the reader to get to the character's thoughts?
questions.q5: Does the point of view hold for the whole scene?

types.first: A character tells the story as “I”: we see only what they see and know only what they know.
types.second: The story addresses a “you” who becomes the protagonist. Rare in novels, common in gamebooks and games.
types.third_limited: Third person, close to one character per scene: we follow their thoughts, but never beyond what they know.
types.third_omniscient: A narrating voice that knows everything: it enters anyone's mind, hints at the future, comments.
types.third_objective: Third person from the outside, like a camera: only actions and dialogue, no thoughts.
types.multiple: Several characters take turns as the point of view, usually a chapter or a scene at a time.

pov.example: The same dinner, seen through Marta in third person limited, gives us her worry for her sister; told by an omniscient voice, it also reveals that her father is lying.

relations.title: Relationships
relations.what: The map of connections among characters, places, objects and groups, each with its kind: family, romance, alliance, rivalry and so on. Seeing the whole web helps you spot hidden tensions and isolated characters.

questions.q2: Which bond is most fragile, and what could break it?
questions.q3: Who knows a secret about someone else?
questions.q4: Which relationships change from beginning to end?
questions.q5: Is anyone isolated? Is that deliberate?

relations.example: Marta and her father: family, but rivals too, because he hid her sister's letters. The fresco belongs to the diocese and is tied to the church of San Silvestro.

groups.title: Groups
groups.what: Families, factions, organisations, cultures: sets of characters, places and objects with their own language, traditions and powers. A well-built group weighs on its members' choices even when it's offstage.

questions.q2: Who's in charge, and who wants to be?
questions.q3: Which rules, rites or words set it apart?
questions.q4: What does it give its members, and what does it ask in return?
questions.q5: Which other groups is it in conflict with?

groups.example: The Cartographers' Guild draws the kingdom's maps and so, in practice, decides its borders. It has a language of symbols, an oath of silence and a seat on the council. Traitors are erased from every map.

timeline.title: Timeline
timeline.what: Scenes and events in chronological order, with date, time and duration, linked to characters, places, objects and real historical events. It's how you catch contradictions before someone else does.

questions.q1: When does each scene take place, and how long does it last?
questions.q2: Where is every character in the meantime?
questions.q3: How much time passes between chapters?
questions.q4: Which real historical events touch the story?
questions.q5: Do the ages, seasons and distances add up?

timeline.example: 14 March 2005, 9 a.m.: Marta finds the portrait. Same day, 9 p.m.: her father burns the letters. In between, a phone call neither of them will remember the same way.

revisions.title: Revisions
revisions.what: Successive versions of a scene, kept side by side. You can rewrite without fear: the previous version stays where it is, and you can go back to it whenever you like.

questions.q1: What do you want to change in this version: the structure, the pace, the voice?
questions.q2: What worked in the previous version and should stay?
questions.q3: Is the scene still doing its job in the story?
questions.q4: What can you cut without losing anything?

revisions.example: Revision 1: the fresco scene in three pages. Revision 2: the same scene in a single page, entirely through Marta's eyes. Keep both and decide later.

branching.title: Branching
branching.what: The links between scenes that depend on the player's choices. Each choice has its own text, can require a condition and can change variables; the graph view shows the flow and flags any scene no one can ever reach.

questions.q1: What is the player choosing, and what do they know at that moment?
questions.q2: Are the options really different, or do they all lead to the same place?
questions.q3: Which consequences show up right away, and which much later?
questions.q4: Where do the branches rejoin, to keep the story manageable?
questions.q5: Can every scene and every ending be reached?

branching.example: At the pier, the player can give Ilse the letter or keep it. “Give her the letter” leads to the lighthouse scene and raises ilse_trust by 1; “Keep it” leads to the market and closes her quest.

variables.title: State variables
variables.what: The game's memory: values that record what the player has done. Each variable has a name, a type (true or false, number, text) and a starting value; choices change it, and conditions read it to open or close a path.

questions.q1: What does the game need to remember about the player's choices?
questions.q2: Is true or false enough, or do you need a number that rises and falls?
questions.q3: What's the starting value, and what changes it?
questions.q4: In which scenes does this variable actually make a difference?
questions.q5: Is the name clear to someone who didn't create it?

variables.example: ilse_trust, a number starting at 0: up by 1 when you help her, down by 2 when you lie to her. If it reaches 3, Ilse tells you about her son at the lighthouse.

codex.title: Lore codex
codex.what: The encyclopaedia of your game's world: history, religions, species, technologies, legends, sorted into categories. It serves you and the team, and it can become the basis of the codex the player unlocks in the game.

questions.q1: What does anyone working on the game need to know about this topic?
questions.q2: What does the player already know, and what will they find out later?
questions.q3: Does this entry contradict anything already written?
questions.q4: Which characters, places or quests refer to it?
questions.q5: What stays a mystery, on purpose?

codex.example: Category History, entry “The Night of Lanterns”: the year the sea drew back for three days. The fishermen remember it as a miracle; the Cartographers, as an error in the maps.

dialogue_lines.title: Dialogue lines
dialogue_lines.what: Dialogue written as a script: for each line, who speaks, what they say and how they say it. Every line gets a unique ID, so voice-over and localisation always know which one you mean.

questions.q1: Who is speaking, and to whom?
questions.q2: What does the character want from this line?
questions.q3: How should it be delivered: whispered, wry, broken?
questions.q4: Does it work when heard, not just read?
questions.q5: Is it short enough to fit in a subtitle?
questions.q6: Does it sound like this character, and no one else?

dialogue_lines.example: Speaker: Ilse. Line: “The lighthouse won't light itself.” Direction: tired, without turning round.

goals.title: Goals
goals.what: A word target for the whole work, a daily one and, if you like, a deadline. Dramatis records what you write day by day and shows you the trend, without judgement.

questions.q1: Roughly how long will the finished work be?
questions.q2: How many words can you write on an ordinary day, not your best one?
questions.q3: Do you have a real deadline, or would one help?
questions.q4: Which days of the week do you actually write?
questions.q5: What counts as work: revising and planning too?

goals.example: An 80,000-word novel at 500 words a day takes about 160 writing days: just over five months if you write every day.
